title: 1975 – Queen – 9 weeks at No. 1 on the UK Singles Chart
clues: A six-minute rock epic without a chorus that reshaped radio’s idea of a single in the mid-’70s.
Its groundbreaking promo clip, directed by Bruce Gowers, helped usher in the modern music-video era.
A headbanging car scene in a 1992 comedy film reignited its U.S. chart success, peaking at No. 2 on the Hot 100.
The operatic middle features dense multi‑track vocal layers and Brian May’s ‘Red Special’ guitar harmonies.
Recorded at Rockfield Studios in Wales in 1975; after its singer’s death in 1991, it returned to No. 1 in the UK.

title: 1980 – AC/DC — RIAA multi‑Platinum single from a 25× Platinum album
clues: An arena-shaking comeback statement released only months after the band lost its original frontman.
Tracked at Compass Point Studios in Nassau with producer Robert John “Mutt” Lange, the mix is famously dry and punchy.
Built around a staccato E–D–A riff by Angus Young that’s among the most instantly recognizable in rock.
Brian Johnson’s lyrics salute survival and legacy — “forget the hearse ’cause I never die” — as a tribute to Bon Scott.
Name the AC/DC anthem whose title combines a color with a bold declaration of return.

title: 1977 — Eagles — US Hot 100 No. 1; won Record of the Year at the 1978 Grammys
clues: A mid-’70s rock epic famed for its haunting atmosphere and a long twin‑guitar coda routinely ranked among the greatest solos ever recorded.
Its storyline follows a weary traveler lured into a glamorous refuge that slowly reveals itself as a gilded cage—often read as a metaphor for 1970s Los Angeles excess and the music industry.
The initial demo carried the working title “Mexican Reggae,” sketched on a 12‑string at a rented Malibu beach house and captured on a TEAC 4‑track.
An enduring urban legend tied it to the Church of Satan, a claim the band publicly denied even as the rumor fueled decades of sensational speculation.
The single topped the US Billboard Hot 100 in May 1977 and later earned Record of the Year at the 1978 Grammy Awards.

title: 1972 – Deep Purple – Peaked at No. 4 on the US Billboard Hot 100
clues: A hard-rock anthem born from a real disaster in a Swiss resort town during an annual music event.
Its album sessions shifted to a grand hotel, tracked with the Rolling Stones Mobile Studio after the intended venue burned down.
The narrative describes a night when a Frank Zappa gig abruptly ended as a flare gun ignited the casino.
The title came from the eerie haze seen drifting across Lake Geneva the following morning.
Built on Ritchie Blackmore’s famous four-note riff, the single later reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1973.

title: 1979 — Pink Floyd — Spent 4 weeks at No. 1 on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100
clues: A rebellious anthem from a concept album that indicts rigid, dehumanizing schooling.
The producer reshaped it with a danceable groove and insisted on adding a children’s chorus to make it single‑ready.
That chant was recorded with pupils from Islington Green School in London, whose involvement later triggered royalty headlines decades on.
It topped the UK chart at Christmas 1979 and then ruled the U.S. Hot 100 for four weeks in 1980.
Adopted by student protesters in apartheid‑era South Africa, it was subsequently banned by the government there.

title: 1971 – Led Zeppelin – Home to a guitar solo voted No. 1 by Guitar World readers
clues: Not issued as a single in the US or UK on release, yet it dominated album‑oriented FM radio programming throughout the 1970s.
Its opening uses layered recorders performed by John Paul Jones, and Robert Plant drafted much of the lyric by the fireplace at Headley Grange.
The band premiered it live at Belfast’s Ulster Hall on March 5, 1971, months before the album reached stores.
It became a flashpoint in the 1980s backmasking scare, with claims of hidden messages when a mid‑section was played backward—claims the group dismissed.
Decades later it faced a high‑profile lawsuit over alleged similarity to Spirit’s “Taurus”; a 2016 jury and a 2020 appeals ruling left the band victorious.

title: 1978 — Dire Straits — Peaked at #4 on the US Billboard Hot 100
clues: A late-’70s debut single that transformed a London pub-rock quartet into international stars.
Its signature lead was played fingerstyle on a Fender Stratocaster—no pick—becoming the guitarist’s calling card.
The lyric’s rainy-night scene came from watching a near-empty South London pub band whose grandiose self-intro inspired the ironic title.
A BBC Radio London DJ (Charlie Gillett) spun the homemade demo on his Honky Tonk show, triggering a rush of label interest and a record deal.
The first cut was done on a shoestring at Pathway Studios; the hit version appeared on the band’s self-titled debut produced by Muff Winwood.

title: 1988 – Guns N’ Roses – first and only US Hot 100 No. 1
clues: A breakout power ballad from a Los Angeles hard‑rock band’s 1987 debut album.
Its shimmering intro began as a string‑skipping warm‑up the lead guitarist once joked about before bandmates urged him to develop it.
The lyrics grew from a poem the singer wrote for his then‑girlfriend Erin Everly, who also appears in the original video.
The song’s famous mid‑section hook came when the vocalist ad‑libbed “Where do we go now?” while the band searched for a transition in the studio.
It topped the Billboard Hot 100 in September 1988, the group’s only U.S. No. 1 single.

title: 1970 — Derek and the Dominos — hit U.S. Billboard Hot 100 Top 10 (1972)
clues: A split‑personality arrangement: blistering twin‑guitar leads up front, then a separate, tape‑spliced piano coda takes over.
Its title and tale of forbidden longing were inspired by the medieval Persian romance Layla and Majnun, discovered just before writing.
Tracked at Criteria Studios in Miami with producer Tom Dowd, it became the definitive anthem of a short‑lived supergroup.
The soaring coda was written and performed by drummer Jim Gordon—later the subject of a public authorship dispute involving Rita Coolidge.
It was Eric Clapton’s confession of love for Pattie Boyd (then George Harrison’s wife), and the single ultimately hit No. 10 in the U.S. in 1972.

title: 1991 — Guns N' Roses — first ’90s music video to surpass 1B views on YouTube
clues: A near nine‑minute power ballad from an L.A. hard‑rock giant’s Use Your Illusion era, instantly global in reach.
Its lavish mini‑movie video—part of a loose trilogy with Don’t Cry and Estranged—tracks a wedding that turns to a funeral in a downpour.
The song grew from Axl Rose’s long‑gestating piano piece and was narratively inspired by Del James’s short story “Without You.”
In 2018, its official video became the first from the 1990s to cross one billion views on YouTube.
Model/actress Stephanie Seymour plays the bride, while Slash rips an iconic desert‑chapel solo on a Les Paul.
